title: Loan Limits for Nursing Grad Students Spark 24-State Lawsuit
summary: A coalition of 24 states and the District of Columbia filed a federal lawsuit Tuesday challenging a Department of Education rule that dramatically limits federal student loans for graduate degrees in nursing and several other healthcare fields. The rule, implementing last year's One Big Beautiful Bill Act, caps annual borrowing for most graduate students at $20,500 with a $100,000 lifetime limit—down from the previous uncapped cost-of-attendance standard. The lawsuit targets the administration's narrow definition of 'professional' degrees eligible for higher limits ($50,000 annually, $200,000 total). The department's list includes only 11 categories: chiropractic, clinical psychology, dentistry, law, medicine, optometry, osteopathic medicine, pharmacy, podiatry, theology, and veterinary medicine. Notably absent are nursing, physical therapy, and nurse anesthesia. 'This rule will shut talented people out of critical professions and leave communities with fewer health care providers they desperately need,' said New York Attorney General Letitia James. The American Nurses Association expressed 'profound dismay,' with president Jennifer Mensik Kennedy warning that in rural areas, nurse practitioners, midwives, and nurse anesthesiologists are often the only providers of core care services. The lawsuit argues the department's list was lifted from a regulation unchanged since the 1950s, 'a time when graduate programs in nursing and other healthcare professions barely existed.' Education Secretary Linda McMahon defended the caps, asserting that most advanced nursing program costs still fall within the new limits and that the caps pressure colleges to lower tuition. However, the American Association of Colleges of Nursing cautioned that students 'could be forced to seek high-interest private loans or abandon advanced practice education.' A study by the conservative American Enterprise Institute downplayed the impact, claiming only a few programs charge 'exorbitant prices.' Yet the bipartisan backlash—including a pointed question from Republican Rep. Randy Fine—signals deep concern over exacerbating healthcare workforce shortages. The outcome could reshape who can afford to enter these essential professions.
why_it_matters: If nursing and physical therapy students can’t get enough federal loans, they may be forced into high‑interest private debt or give up their career plans—leaving hospitals, schools, and rural clinics understaffed, which directly affects the care you and your family receive when you’re sick.

background_read: Federal student loans are the main way many Americans pay for graduate school. Before the One Big Beautiful Bill Act was passed in 2024, students in most graduate programs could borrow up to the full cost of attendance, including living expenses—a system that let them take on debt but ensured they could enroll. The new law rewrote those rules and gave the Secretary of Education power to define which programs count as “professional” degrees, a category that enjoys higher loan caps because such careers are seen as public investments.

The definition being challenged was based on a regulation from the 1950s, when advanced nursing programs barely existed. At that time, a nurse typically earned a diploma in a hospital, not a master’s or doctoral degree. Today, nurse practitioners, nurse midwives, and nurse anesthesiologists (who can deliver anesthesia independently in many rural hospitals) all require graduate education that can cost tens of thousands of dollars. States like New York, California, and Texas argue that sticking to a mid‑20th‑century list unfairly shuts out modern healthcare fields.

The lawsuit includes the District of Columbia and a bipartisan group of states from Hawai‘i to Massachusetts. Groups such as the American Nurses Association (the largest professional organization for U.S. nurses) warn that caps will worsen healthcare workforce shortages—especially in rural areas where nurse practitioners are often the only accessible provider. Meanwhile, a conservative think tank, the American Enterprise Institute, argued only a handful of programs charge “exorbitant” prices, so the impact might be small. The case could decide who can afford to fill critical healthcare jobs for the next generation.

└─ specific: The rule implements the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, capping annual borrowing at $20,500 and lifetime at $100,000 for most graduate students.
CORE DISPUTE: The rule’s narrow definition of 'professional' degrees—only 11 categories—excludes nursing, physical therapy, and nurse anesthesia.
├─ HISTORICAL ROOTS: The list is lifted from a regulation unchanged since the 1950s, when advanced nursing programs barely existed.
└─ CONSEQUENCES: Critics say this will limit who can enter these fields and worsen provider shortages, especially in rural areas.

CRITICS' ARGUMENT: New York Attorney General Letitia James and the American Nurses Association decry the rule, warning that rural nurse practitioners and midwives—often the only local providers—will be hardest hit.
DEFENSE: Education Secretary Linda McMahon says most nursing program costs still fall within the caps and that limiting loans pressures schools to lower tuition.
COUNTERPOINTS: A conservative think tank downplays the impact, but bipartisan voices (including Republican Rep. Randy Fine) signal deep worry about healthcare workforce gaps.
STAKES: The lawsuit’s outcome could determine who can afford to enter essential healthcare professions, shaping the accessibility of care in communities nationwide.

perspectives.description: Proponents argue that limiting loans will force universities to cut inflated tuition and reduce student debt dependence. If a program’s cost is truly reasonable, the new caps should cover it, and students won’t be trapped by loans they can never repay.

Opponents warn the rule will shut talented, lower‑income students out of advanced nursing and therapy careers just when an aging population desperately needs more providers. Rural areas, already suffering shortages, will lose nurse practitioners who are often the only source of primary care.

The case reveals how decades‑old bureaucratic definitions can have sudden, massive consequences. A 1950s list, originally designed when few nurses earned graduate degrees, is now being used to decide which 21st‑century professions are 'professional'—showing how policy inertia can collide with modern workforce needs.

The lawsuit could force Congress to update the professional degree categories or spur states to create their own loan‑forgiveness programs for healthcare workers. Either way, the battle highlights an ongoing tension: who should carry the cost of training the people who keep society healthy?
